title: The universe in your gut
text: The average person carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human ones, a fact that took medicine a surprisingly long time to absorb. For most of the twentieth century, microbes appeared in medical thinking chiefly as {{1}} (ENEMY) to be eliminated with antibiotics, and the notion that a healthy body might {{2}} (ACTIVE) cultivate its own germs seemed absurd. Gene sequencing has overturned that assumption. Surveys of the gut's {{3}} (MICROBE) residents reveal thriving ecosystems that assist {{4}} (DIGEST), train the immune system and manufacture vitamins the diet alone cannot supply. More {{5}} (SURPRISE) still, gut bacteria appear to influence mood: mice raised without any microbes behave {{6}} (DIFFERENT) from ordinary animals, leaping fearlessly where normal mice hesitate, and transplanting gut bacteria can transfer a whole {{7}} (PERSON) from one animal to another, timidity included. Researchers are now exploring what this means for humans, with early trials of so-called psychobiotics under way. The {{8}} (IMPLY) are far-reaching: if the mind's chemistry depends partly on our microbes, then psychiatry's future may lie not only in the brain but in the gut.

gaps.explanation: 'chiefly as enemies to be eliminated' — plural of enemy.
'the gut's microbial residents' — adjective from microbe.
'more surprisingly still' — sentence adverb from surprise.
'transfer a whole personality' — noun from person.
'The implications are far-reaching' — plural pinned by 'are'.
